problem.title: Large-scale document classification
problem.context: An insurer receives two to eight million personal documents daily and classifies them into 60 claim types with an approved EU-region LLM. Three teams consume the results, and storm season creates four times the usual load.

requirements.text: Classify every incoming document into a claim type, with a confidence.
Deliver the results to the three consuming teams.
Send the documents the classifier is unsure about to human review, and use the reviewers' corrections to improve the classifier.
During storm season, at eight million documents a day, every document is classified within two hours of arrival.
When classification quality drops for one claim type (for example, after a form changes its layout), operators see it within one day.
The classification costs less than 0.2 cents per document on average over the year.
A consuming team can change how it processes the results without the other teams or the classifier having to change.
The documents contain personal data and may not leave the EU.
The classifier uses an LLM from the insurer's approved provider, in its EU region.

points.description: A shared data store receives continuously streamed data through a message/event-queue access API, while a dedicated, partitioned processing component prepares data for model building and supports parallel execution. Models are served through a hybrid online/offline approach, tested for quality, monitored in production, and manually adjusted and redeployed when performance results warrant changes.

A continuous stream of incoming data is partitioned within the data pipeline so multiple processing tasks can operate in parallel. Model predictions or scores are then served through a hybrid approach, combining service-based online results with batch-based offline results.
Newly available data is exposed through queued messages or events, allowing services to consume it for online prediction or scoring. Accumulated data can also be processed in offline batches.
The pipeline tests trained model quality before deployment, while production monitoring observes specified model-performance parameters after deployment.
The pipeline tests trained model quality before deployment. Once deployed, the model has no in-production monitoring or tracking.
The data provider is accessed directly, while model predictions or scores are delivered through a hybrid approach combining online services and offline batches.

trajectory.hypothesis: The mapped choices together describe the built classification system.
trajectory.observation: The combination is coherent and has no point warnings or unmet required dimensions. It captures the event stream, processing and result delivery, quality monitoring and human-directed improvement. The point's generated description is a summary, not evidence. The space does not represent the location and provider constraints, costs, prompt details or the quantitative service targets, so those judgments come from the solution text.

trajectory.hypothesis: R1 and Q1 explain streaming ingestion, parallel processing and mixed serving for high-volume classification.
trajectory.observation: The point describes a compatible route for continuous arrivals, parallel processing and online plus batch results. It supports the shape of the scale strategy, but the two-hour target and eight-million daily volume are not established by these values.

trajectory.hypothesis: R2 and Q4 explain queued result access and the serving arrangement for independent consumers.
trajectory.observation: Queued messages and hybrid serving fit asynchronous consumption; the solution specifies separate consumer groups, letting teams process at their own pace. The contrast with direct provider access remains compatible with serving but offers no equivalent queue-mediated decoupling, so the requirements support the chosen access pattern.

trajectory.hypothesis: Q2 explains production monitoring and checking the classifier's quality before changing its prompt.
trajectory.observation: Monitoring per-claim-type review share and confidence, plus testing a candidate prompt against reviewed documents, directly address detection and quality validation. The point without monitoring misses Q2, showing that production monitoring is required; the space does not express the one-day threshold or alert calculation.

trajectory.hypothesis: Does Q2 force production monitoring rather than no in-production monitoring?
trajectory.observation: With no in-production monitoring the combination cannot reveal a claim-type quality drop within one day. The requirement forces the monitoring choice.

trajectory.hypothesis: Does Q4 force queued access rather than direct access?
trajectory.observation: Direct access with hybrid serving is compatible but does not itself provide the separate asynchronous result channel described by the solution. Since the space offers no explicit consumer-group value, Q4 supports the queueing choice but does not prove it is the only way to decouple consumers; treat it as supported rather than strictly forced.

regions.name: Queued results for independent consumers
regions.reason: The event queue and hybrid serving fit delivering results to multiple consumers asynchronously. Separate consumer groups in the solution make the loose-coupling mechanism concrete.

regions.name: Quality checks and production signals
regions.reason: The solution monitors claim-type signals in production and validates prompt changes against reviewed examples; the no-monitoring contrast fails the observability need.

regions.name: Streamed parallel classification
regions.reason: Continuous ingestion, parallel work and mixed delivery support the high-volume workflow, although the quantitative deadline is not guaranteed by the mapped values.

alternatives.name: Document classification as built
alternatives.summary: An event-driven, parallel classification pipeline uses an approved EU LLM, fans results out through Kafka, and learns from human review with monitored, tested prompt updates.

choices.reason: The EU object store holds source documents and extracted text for the workflow. The space does not decide data residency.
choices.solution_quote: Incoming documents land in an object storage bucket in the EU region

choices.reason: Kafka topics provide queued result access and separate consumer groups. Queueing is supported by loose coupling, though the space does not establish it as the only viable design.
choices.solution_quote: Each consuming team has its own consumer group and reads at its own pace

choices.reason: Streaming classification and hourly warehouse loading combine service-like and batch delivery. This is an approximate fit because the mapped value describes hybrid serving, not specifically asynchronous Kafka output.
choices.fit_note: Kafka result events and the hourly warehouse load are not explicitly distinguished as online/offline model serving in the space.
choices.solution_quote: Results go to a second Kafka topic. Each consuming team has its own consumer group and reads at its own pace; analytics also loads the topic into the data warehouse every hour.

choices.reason: Every upload emits an event that starts a continuously available processing flow, matching streamed ingestion.
choices.solution_quote: each upload puts a message on a Kafka topic

choices.reason: A dedicated preprocessing service extracts text, runs OCR and removes duplicates, matching a data processing component.
choices.solution_quote: A preprocessing service reads the topic, extracts the text (with OCR for scanned forms), removes duplicates by content hash and writes the text next to the document.

choices.reason: Classifier workers scale with backlog and process independent documents in parallel, approximating partitioned parallel processing.
choices.fit_note: The solution scales Kafka consumers but does not state explicit data partitioning within a pipeline.
choices.solution_quote: The number of classifier workers scales with the length of the Kafka topic's backlog, from 4 to 120.

choices.reason: Per-claim-type review share and confidence provide production performance signals; omitting monitoring fails the one-day quality visibility need.
choices.solution_quote: A dashboard shows, per claim type, the share of documents sent to review and the mean confidence; an alert fires when the share sent to review for a claim type doubles from one week to the next.

choices.reason: Claims staff correct uncertain results and the team manually updates the prompt using those corrections. This is a rough match to manual model adjustment, since the adjusted artifact is a prompt rather than model parameters.
choices.fit_note: Prompt example replacement is not expressly represented by the model adjustment value.
choices.solution_quote: Every month the team replaces the prompt's examples with recent corrected documents

choices.reason: The candidate prompt is checked against reviewed documents before it is switched, testing classification quality.
choices.solution_quote: checks the new prompt against 2,000 reviewed documents before switching to it

adrs.title: Ingest and process documents as a scalable event flow
adrs.context: The classifier must handle continuous arrivals and storm peaks. Events trigger preprocessing and a backlog drives additional classifier workers.

options.name: Streamed, component-based parallel processing
pros: Supports continuous intake and independent processing work.
Backlog-based scaling responds to changing load.
cons: The design space value does not guarantee the two-hour deadline or maximum volume.
options.reason: Chosen to support R1 and Q1; the exact throughput target depends on capacity and provider limits not represented in the space.

adrs.title: Distribute results through queued channels
adrs.context: Three teams need results and must be able to change their processing independently.

options.name: Queued result access with hybrid delivery
pros: Consumer groups can read independently at their own pace.
The warehouse can consume the stream on its separate hourly schedule.
cons: Consumers receive event-based results rather than a uniform request response.
options.reason: The requirements support this asynchronous design; the user expressly chose Kafka consumer groups, while the space does not establish the choice as uniquely forced.

options.name: Direct data access with hybrid serving
pros: Direct access is compatible with hybrid serving.
cons: Does not itself provide independent queued consumption.
options.reason: This space alternative does not explain the loose-coupled consumer arrangement as well. It is a contrast offered by the space, not a stated option the designers weighed.

adrs.title: Observe and validate classification quality
adrs.context: Operators must see claim-type quality changes within a day, and prompt changes need a check against reviewed cases.

options.name: Production performance monitoring with model quality tests
pros: Per-type signals reveal changes in the operational workflow.
Reviewed-document validation checks prompt revisions before release.
cons: The weekly sample and week-over-week alert do not ensure visibility within one day for every quality drop.
options.reason: Production monitoring is forced by Q2. The solution's specific signals and thresholds are design choices beyond what the mapped values specify.

options.name: No in-production monitoring with model quality tests
pros: Pre-release model quality testing remains possible.
cons: Cannot provide production visibility into claim-type quality changes.
options.reason: It misses Q2 and is rejected by the requirement. This contrast is an option in the space, not one the designers said they considered.

adrs.title: Use human corrections to adjust classification
adrs.context: Uncertain documents need human correction, and those corrections must improve subsequent classification.

options.name: Manual adjustment from reviewed corrections
pros: Claims staff supply corrected labels and recent examples inform the next prompt.
cons: Monthly prompt refresh is not immediate learning and can lag new document patterns.
options.reason: R3 requires human review and reuse of corrections. The solution's monthly, tested prompt update is one implementation; the space's manual adjustment value is approximate.

adrs.title: Retain documents and extracted text in shared storage
adrs.context: The pipeline needs durable access to incoming documents and extracted text for classification and result use.

options.name: Shared data store
pros: The source object and extracted text remain available to the processing flow.
cons: The space does not capture EU residency, access controls or retention policy.
options.reason: The solution uses shared object storage, matching this value. The choice is not forced by a requirement represented in this dimension.

uncovered.decision: EU data residency and the approved provider's EU-region LLM
uncovered.solution_quote: The classifier service, running on Kubernetes, sends the text to the approved provider's LLM in its EU region.

uncovered.decision: Prompt design, confidence threshold, and batching small documents for provider cost control
uncovered.solution_quote: Small documents are sent in batches of 20 to reduce cost.

uncovered.decision: Kubernetes deployment and backlog-based worker autoscaling
uncovered.solution_quote: The number of classifier workers scales with the length of the Kafka topic's backlog, from 4 to 120.

uncovered.decision: Versioning each result with prompt version and model name
uncovered.solution_quote: Every result is stored with the prompt version and the model name that produced it.

uncovered.decision: Confidence threshold routing and labelling-tool review queue
uncovered.solution_quote: Documents with a confidence below 0.7 go to a review queue in a labelling tool, where claims staff correct the claim type.

uncovered.decision: Per-type review-share alerts and weekly random audit sampling
uncovered.solution_quote: Each week, analysts review a random sample of 300 classified documents.

unaddressed.note: The space has no cost dimension. Batching is described as reducing cost, but the 0.2-cent annual target cannot be assessed from its values.
The space has no dimension for data residency or personal-data jurisdiction.
The space has no dimension for approved-provider selection or provider region.
